PHASE 3 · ADVANCED HEALTH ASSESSMENT & CLINICAL DIAGNOSTICS

Week 43 — Lesson 67: Neurologic Health Assessment & Diagnostics

FNP-level goal: Evaluate neurologic symptoms through stability, time course, localization, focused examination, and diagnostic safety. Distinguish common outpatient syndromes from time-sensitive stroke/TIA, hemorrhage, CNS infection, seizure emergency, spinal cord disease, and toxic-metabolic illness; then choose the correct urgency, testing question, consultation, and safety net.

Learning Objectives

  • Recognize neurologic red flags that require emergency evaluation rather than an extended outpatient workup.
  • Use onset, trajectory, and anatomic localization to create a focused differential.
  • Perform and document a practical focused neurologic examination.
  • Approach headache, dizziness, weakness/numbness, altered mental status, and seizure without anchoring on a benign label.
  • Select laboratories, ECG, imaging, and referral to answer a defined clinical question.
  • Provide reliable follow-up and return precautions when outpatient care is appropriate.

Part 1 — Neurologic Symptoms Begin With Time and Stability

First ask: When was the patient last known well? A new sudden focal deficit, new aphasia, facial asymmetry, unilateral weakness/numbness, acute visual loss, severe imbalance, altered consciousness, seizure with incomplete recovery, thunderclap headache, meningismus with systemic illness, or rapidly progressive weakness may represent a neurologic emergency. Assess airway, breathing, circulation, glucose when clinically indicated, vital signs, mental status, trauma risk, anticoagulant use, and whether the patient can safely remain in clinic.

Do not wait for every examination maneuver, a routine outpatient imaging order, or symptom resolution before escalating a suspected stroke, TIA, intracranial hemorrhage, spinal cord emergency, or status epilepticus. Sudden neurologic symptoms can improve and still indicate TIA or stroke risk. Emergency transport and local acute-stroke pathways take priority when indicated.

Part 2 — Build a Neurologic Problem Representation

Describe the symptom precisely: sudden or gradual; maximum intensity at onset or progressive; episodic, persistent, or fluctuating; focal or diffuse; positive symptoms such as tingling, flashing lights, or jerking versus negative symptoms such as weakness, numbness, loss of vision, or inability to speak. Ask about headache, neck pain, fever, trauma, exertion, positional change, palpitations, chest symptoms, dyspnea, syncope, vomiting, medication/substance exposure, pregnancy/postpartum status, diabetes, vascular risk, cancer, immune compromise, and prior episodes.

Then localize provisionally. Cortical processes may cause aphasia, neglect, visual-field loss, or focal deficits; brainstem/cerebellar processes may cause diplopia, dysarthria, severe gait ataxia, or crossed findings; peripheral nerve, root, neuromuscular, muscle, metabolic, and medication causes have different patterns. Localization organizes urgency and testing but is not a substitute for emergency evaluation when a high-consequence diagnosis remains plausible.

Part 3 — Focused Neurologic Examination

Start with general appearance, level of arousal, orientation, speech quality, language comprehension, attention, and ability to follow commands. Assess pupils, eye movements, facial symmetry, visual fields when feasible, articulation, tongue/palate, and swallowing concern. Compare motor strength, pronator drift, tone, sensation, coordination, reflexes when relevant, and gait only if safe. Observe for nystagmus, tremor, involuntary movements, neglect, or a change from baseline.

Document what you actually observe: for example, “new right arm pronator drift and word-finding difficulty, last known well 09:10,” not simply “neuro abnormal.” A normal brief examination does not exclude TIA, posterior-circulation ischemia, evolving stroke, intermittent seizure, early CNS infection, or an episodic arrhythmia. Repeat the examination if symptoms change.

Part 4 — Acute Focal Deficit and TIA

Stroke symptoms usually occur suddenly. Key warning patterns include new facial droop, arm or leg weakness/numbness on one side, language disturbance, visual loss, severe new imbalance, or a severe unexplained headache. Symptoms that resolve within minutes may be a TIA, not a harmless event. Capture last-known-well time, anticoagulants/antiplatelets, baseline function, glucose when indicated, and the exact symptom sequence; then activate the appropriate emergency pathway.

Stroke mimics exist, including hypoglycemia, seizure with postictal deficits, migraine aura, functional symptoms, infection, and medication effects. The FNP safety principle is not to diagnose a mimic before addressing a plausible acute vascular event. A risk factor profile does not rule stroke in or out; young, pregnant/postpartum, and otherwise healthy patients can also have time-sensitive neurologic disease.

Part 5 — Headache: Primary Pattern or Secondary Threat?

Ask about first or worst headache, thunderclap onset, onset during exertion/sex/cough, new neurologic deficit, fever or neck stiffness, altered mental status, trauma, cancer, immune compromise, pregnancy/postpartum context, anticoagulants, age at new onset, change in established pattern, visual symptoms, and signs of increased intracranial pressure. A sudden severe headache reaching maximum intensity immediately requires emergency assessment for dangerous secondary causes.

Stable recurrent headache with a typical established migraine pattern and normal neurologic examination may be managed differently from headache with red flags. Imaging is not a reflex for every uncomplicated headache; it should answer a defined question and follow current guidance. A red flag changes the disposition first—do not use outpatient imaging as a substitute for emergency evaluation when hemorrhage, infection, stroke, or another acute process is possible.

Part 6 — Dizziness Is a Symptom, Not a Diagnosis

Clarify what the patient means: spinning/vertigo, near-syncope, imbalance, nonspecific lightheadedness, or visual motion sensitivity. Define timing, triggers, duration, hearing symptoms, vomiting, headache/neck pain, palpitations, chest symptoms, medication changes, orthostatic symptoms, gait ability, and new focal neurologic symptoms. Dizziness with inability to walk safely, new focal deficit, severe headache/neck pain, persistent severe vomiting, syncope, or high-risk cardiovascular features requires urgent escalation.

Peripheral vestibular disease is common, but a reassuring-sounding word such as “vertigo” does not exclude a central or cardiovascular cause. Do not rely on one isolated bedside sign outside appropriate training, context, and local pathway. Combine the whole history, gait, ocular findings, focused neurologic examination, cardiovascular assessment, and trajectory.

Part 7 — Weakness and Numbness: Central, Peripheral, or Systemic?

Determine true weakness versus pain-limited effort, fatigue, dyspnea, dizziness, or sensory change. Ask whether onset was sudden; whether symptoms are unilateral, bilateral, proximal, distal, ascending, symmetric, intermittent, or associated with back/neck pain, bowel/bladder dysfunction, saddle sensory change, cranial symptoms, myalgias, fever, rash, or recent infection. Compare sides and functional tasks when safe.

Sudden unilateral weakness, aphasia, or facial droop suggests an acute central process until proven otherwise. Rapidly progressive weakness, respiratory symptoms, bulbar symptoms, new bowel/bladder dysfunction, saddle anesthesia, or suspected spinal cord compression/cauda equina syndrome requires emergency assessment. Metabolic causes, medication effects, neuropathy, radiculopathy, myopathy, and functional symptoms may be considered only after time-sensitive alternatives are addressed.

Part 8 — Altered Mental Status and Delirium

Altered mental status is a syndrome, not a final diagnosis. Establish baseline cognition and the exact onset. Consider oxygenation/ventilation, glucose, infection, medication or substance exposure, withdrawal, electrolyte/renal/hepatic disturbance, stroke, seizure, trauma, pain, urinary retention, and environmental change. In older adults, delirium can be the first sign of serious systemic illness and should not be dismissed as “normal aging.”

Fluctuating attention and acute change from baseline support delirium, but they do not identify the cause. Obtain collateral history, review all prescriptions/OTC agents/supplements, and assess immediate safety. New severe confusion, decreased level of consciousness, focal findings, fever/meningismus, hypoxia, unstable vital signs, or concern for poisoning/withdrawal needs emergency evaluation.

Part 9 — Seizure and Transient Loss of Consciousness

Obtain a witness description: onset, focal signs, duration, awareness, motor activity, eye position, color change, tongue injury, incontinence, injury, recovery, and postevent confusion. Clarify prior seizures, missed antiseizure medication, sleep deprivation, alcohol/substance use or withdrawal, fever, head injury, pregnancy, diabetes, and cardiac symptoms. Syncope can include brief abnormal movements; a label of “seizure” should not end the cardiovascular, metabolic, and neurologic differential.

Protect airway and the patient from injury, time the event, and follow local emergency protocols. Emergency help is indicated for a first seizure, seizure lasting more than five minutes, repeated seizures, injury, pregnancy, breathing difficulty, persistent impaired recovery, or other instability. Do not place objects in the person’s mouth or restrain them during a convulsive seizure.

Part 10 — Diagnostics: Test a Question, Not a Symptom

Point-of-care glucose, ECG, pulse oximetry, pregnancy testing when relevant, and selected CBC, electrolytes, renal/hepatic studies, toxicology or drug levels, infection studies, and other labs may be useful when they answer a hypothesis. ECG matters when near-syncope, palpitations, exertional symptoms, or arrhythmia risk may explain a neurologic presentation. A medication reconciliation is part of the diagnostic workup, especially for sedatives, anticholinergics, stimulants, anticoagulants, hypoglycemics, antihypertensives, and substances.

CT, MRI, vascular imaging, EEG, lumbar puncture, and specialty testing have distinct roles. The FNP task is to identify the question and urgency—not to delay transfer of an unstable patient while arranging an outpatient study. Use current local stroke, seizure, headache, pregnancy, and imaging pathways, and coordinate with emergency, neurology, or other services when appropriate.

Part 11 — Clinical Case: Brief Deficit Does Not Mean No Emergency

A 69-year-old with hypertension and atrial fibrillation suddenly develops left arm weakness and slurred speech while eating breakfast. The symptoms are nearly resolved by arrival.

FNP reasoning: sudden focal symptoms with partial resolution are compatible with TIA or evolving stroke. Record last known well and exact sequence; assess stability; and arrange emergency stroke evaluation. Resolution is diagnostic information, not a reason to wait for a routine clinic appointment.

Part 12 — Clinical Case: “Vertigo” With a Dangerous Pattern

A 63-year-old reports abrupt persistent dizziness, repeated vomiting, severe unsteadiness, and new trouble walking. They have diabetes and cannot ambulate safely without support.

FNP reasoning: a peripheral vestibular syndrome is possible, but severe gait impairment and acute persistent symptoms require assessment for central and other high-consequence causes. Treat disposition as the priority; do not use a benign vestibular label to defer evaluation.

Part 13 — Clinical Case: First Convulsion

A 34-year-old has no seizure history and experienced a witnessed convulsive episode lasting about two minutes, followed by persistent confusion. The family reports a new severe headache earlier that day.

FNP reasoning: this is not simply a medication-refill or outpatient EEG question. First seizure, persistent postevent abnormality, and new severe headache require urgent emergency assessment for structural, infectious, vascular, metabolic, toxic, and other causes.

FNP Neurologic-Assessment Framework

  1. Stabilize and time-stamp: ABCs, glucose when indicated, vital signs, last known well, baseline, trauma, anticoagulants, and safety for transfer.
  2. Characterize: sudden/gradual, focal/diffuse, positive/negative symptoms, triggers, and trajectory.
  3. Localize provisionally: cortical, brainstem/cerebellar, spinal, peripheral, neuromuscular, metabolic, toxic, or systemic.
  4. Examine and document: mental status, speech/language, cranial findings, motor, sensory, coordination, and safe gait assessment.
  5. Protect against anchors: migraine, vertigo, anxiety, “old age,” or a prior diagnosis cannot safely explain a changed or red-flag presentation.
  6. Test with a question: glucose, ECG, targeted labs, imaging, EEG, or specialty assessment based on urgency and differential.
  7. Close the loop: explicit return precautions, result ownership, reliable follow-up, and immediate escalation for new or worsening deficits.

High-Yield Summary

Sudden focal neurologic symptoms: are a stroke/TIA emergency until appropriately assessed, even if they resolve.
Headache: screen for sudden maximal onset, focal deficit, fever/meningismus, trauma, pregnancy context, immune compromise, cancer, anticoagulation, and pattern change.
Dizziness: specify the sensation, timing, triggers, gait ability, neurologic signs, and cardiovascular context; “vertigo” is not a diagnosis.
Weakness: distinguish true weakness from fatigue and recognize spinal, bulbar, respiratory, or bowel/bladder red flags.
Altered mental status: demands baseline comparison, medication review, collateral history, and systemic/toxic/metabolic/neurologic evaluation.
Seizure: obtain a witness history and escalate a first, prolonged, recurrent, injurious, pregnancy-associated, breathing-compromised, or incompletely recovered event.
FNP standard: integrate time course, localization, risk, examination, testing purpose, disposition, and safety netting.

Clinical safety note: This lesson is educational. Neurologic assessment, stroke/TIA response, headache evaluation, seizure care, imaging, treatment, referral, and follow-up must follow current evidence, local protocols, scope requirements, and the individual patient’s presentation.
